category.text: $course$/Containerization in AWS/Track A — ECS & Fargate Quiz

name.text: CA01 — Why the Containers Use Public Subnets

questiontext.text: Your VPC has two public subnets and two private subnets, and it has no NAT Gateway. Your ECS tasks run in the public subnets with public IP addresses, while the RDS database runs in the private subnets. Why do the ECS tasks need to run in the public subnets instead of the private ones?

answer.text: Without a NAT Gateway, a task in a private subnet has no route to the internet, so it could not pull its image from ECR or reach AWS APIs.
An Application Load Balancer can only forward traffic to targets that are in public subnets.
RDS only accepts database connections from resources that are in public subnets.
Private subnets are billed by the hour, while public subnets are free to use.

name.text: CA02 — Passing an Ephemeral Password to RDS

questiontext.text: In your infra/20-data stack, you read the database password from Secrets Manager with an ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" block, and you want to pass it to aws_db_instance without it ever being saved in Terraform state. Which approach works?

answer.text: Pass it to the write-only argument password_wo together with password_wo_version, because ephemeral values are only allowed in write-only arguments, which are never saved to state.
Pass it to the normal password argument, because Terraform automatically encrypts any value that comes from an ephemeral block.
Pass it to the normal password argument and mark that argument as sensitive, which keeps the value out of the state file.
Pass only the username, because RDS reads the matching password from Secrets Manager on its own once it knows the user.

questiontext.text: You create a brand-new RDS for PostgreSQL 17 instance, and your security groups correctly allow port 5432 from the app tier. When the backend starts, it logs the error no pg_hba.conf entry … no encryption and cannot connect. What is causing the error?

answer.text: RDS for PostgreSQL 15 and later requires TLS by default (rds.force_ssl = 1), and the backend is trying to connect without encryption.
Port 5432 is actually blocked, so the connection falls back to an unencrypted port that RDS rejects.
The password stored in Secrets Manager does not match the password set on the database.
The DB subnet group uses public subnets, and RDS refuses connections to instances placed in public subnets.

name.text: CA04 — Which Role Fetches the Password

questiontext.text: Your backend task definition gets DB_PASSWORD through its secrets block, and the application code itself never calls any AWS API. When a new backend task starts, which IAM role actually reads the secret from Secrets Manager?

answer.text: The task execution role reads it, because ECS uses that role to prepare the task before your code starts running.
The backend's task role reads it, because the environment variable ends up inside the backend container.
The ECS infrastructure role for load balancers reads it, because it manages everything the service needs at start-up.
The GitLab CI role reads it, because it registers the task definition that contains the secret reference.

name.text: CA05 — A Request for /api With No Trailing Slash

questiontext.text: Your ALB listener has one rule with the path pattern /api/* that forwards to the backend, and a default action that forwards to the frontend. A request arrives for exactly /api, with no trailing slash. Where does the ALB send it?

answer.text: The ALB sends it to the frontend through the default action, because the pattern /api/* does not match /api on its own.
The ALB sends it to the backend, because the ALB adds a trailing slash to the path before it checks the rules.
The ALB returns a 404 error itself, because no listener rule matched the request.
The ALB splits the request evenly between the frontend and backend target groups.

name.text: CA06 — The Backend Scaled to Zero

questiontext.text: You scale the dcta-backend ECS service down to 0 tasks, but the /api/* listener rule still exists and still forwards to the backend target group. What does a browser get back when it requests GET /api/tasks?

answer.text: It gets a 503 error, because the rule matched but its target group has no registered targets to send the request to.
It gets the React page with a 200 status, because the ALB falls back to the default action when a target group is empty.
It gets a 404 error from the ALB, because the backend path no longer exists once the service has no tasks.
The request times out, because the security group still points at the IP address of the old task.

name.text: CA07 — Terraform After a Pipeline Deploy

questiontext.text: GitLab CI has just deployed task definition revision 7 to the dcta-backend service. The service's Terraform code does not include lifecycle { ignore_changes = [task_definition] }. You now run terraform apply on 30-track-a to change something unrelated. What happens to the backend service?

answer.text: Terraform points the service back at the task definition revision it knows about, which undoes the deployment the pipeline just made.
Nothing happens to the service, because Terraform never checks which task definition revision a service is using.
Terraform stops with a drift error and refuses to apply any changes until the drift is fixed by hand.
Terraform adopts revision 7 as its own and keeps it running from now on.

name.text: CA08 — A CI Job on a Feature Branch

questiontext.text: Your GitLab CI jobs log in to AWS with OIDC. The dcta-gitlab-ci role trusts only tokens whose gitlab.com:sub is project_path:<group>/<project>:ref_type:branch:ref:main. A job running on the branch feature/login fails with not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Why does the job fail?

answer.text: The job's OIDC token says it comes from the feature/login branch, and the role only trusts tokens that come from the main branch.
The AWS access key stored in the GitLab CI/CD variables has expired and needs to be rotated.
OIDC tokens are only issued to scheduled pipelines, not to pipelines triggered by a push.
The role's permission policy does not include ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, so the login step is refused.

name.text: CA09 — Scaling on the Average, Not the Maximum

questiontext.text: Your backend service auto-scales with a target-tracking policy on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization at 70%. It is currently running 3 tasks, and their CPU use is 90%, 20% and 20%. What will auto scaling do?

answer.text: It will not scale out, because the service's average CPU is about 43%, which is below the 70% target.
It will scale out, because one of the tasks is running above the 70% target.
It will replace the task that is at 90% CPU with a new task.
It will jump straight to the maximum number of tasks, because one task is 20 points over the target.

name.text: CA10 — Two Different Answers During a Deploy

questiontext.text: During a blue/green deployment of the backend, a plain curl /api/tasks returns the old version, but curl -H 'X-Deploy-Stage: test' /api/tasks returns the new version. Why do the two requests get different versions?

answer.text: A higher-priority test rule matches the header and forwards to the alternate target group where the new tasks run, while the production rule has not switched yet.
The ALB caches the old response for any request that does not carry a custom header.
Sticky sessions keep normal users on the old tasks until they end their session.
The header sends the request to a second load balancer that ECS creates for the length of the deployment.
